extracted.intended_audience: trademark practitioners and parties in TTAB inter partes proceedings (attorneys, litigants before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural rules and practical guidance for noticing, taking, and enforcing discovery depositions in inter partes proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, including domestic and foreign depositions, written-question depositions, subpoena practice, and related cooperation duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of discovery depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be both noticed and taken prior to the expiration of the discovery period (unless the parties stipulate that the deposition may be taken outside of the period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositions must be taken (not merely served) during the discovery period; parties may stipulate otherwise. See notes comparing Fed. R. Civ. P. 30 and 33 (interrogatories served vs depositions taken).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may take depositions / who may be deposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions generally may be taken by any party, of any adverse party or any relevant non-party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may, by oral questions, depose any person, including a party, without leave of court except as provided in Rule 30(a)(2). The deponent's attendance may be compelled by subpoena under Rule 45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate in scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should attempt to schedule depositions by agreement rather than have the deposing party unilaterally set a deposition date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a matter of convenience and courtesy and to avoid scheduling conflicts, parties should attempt to agree on dates; although it is not unusual for a deposing party to notice a deposition and then discuss alternatives. See TBMP § 408 regarding cooperation obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances requiring leave of court / Board permission
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must obtain leave of court (and the court must grant leave consistent with Rule 26(b)(2)) if: (i) the deposition would result in more than 10 depositions by plaintiffs/defendants/third-party defendants without stipulation; (ii) the deponent has already been deposed; (iii) the party seeks to take the deposition before the time specified in Rule 26(d) (unless notice certifies, with supporting facts, that the deponent will leave the U.S. and be unavailable); or (B) if the deponent is confined in prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board's permission must be obtained under similar circumstances: prisoner deponents, proposed >10 depositions without stipulation, or deponent already deposed. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a)(2) and related TBMP notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposition location for persons residing in the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposition of a natural person shall be taken in the Federal judicial district where the person resides or is regularly employed or at any place on which the parties agree by stipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to discovery depositions in Board proceedings (37 CFR § 2.120(b)). If parties agree, deposition may be elsewhere. See Jain v. Ramparts Inc. and Fed. R. Civ. P. 30 and 31 for background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of deposition: oral or written questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition may be taken either orally, or on written questions in the manner described in 37 CFR § 2.124.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For taking discovery depositions on written questions see TBMP § 404.07 and the specific provisions of 37 CFR § 2.124. Written-question depositions have particular service and filing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party deponents in the United States — notice and compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed deponent residing in the United States is a party (or an officer/director/managing agent of a party or a Rule 30(b)(6) designee), the deposition may be taken on notice alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a proposed deponent fails to appear for a noticed deposition, the deposing party may seek to compel attendance by a motion to compel (see TBMP § 523).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonparty deponents in the United States — securing attendance and subpoenas
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed deponent in the United States is not a party (or officer/director/managing agent or Rule 30(b)(6) designee), the deposing party is wholly responsible to secure attendance; if not willing to appear voluntarily, attendance must be secured by subpoena under Fed. R. Civ. P. 45 and 35 U.S.C. § 24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subpoena must be issued from the U.S. district court in the federal judicial district where the deponent resides or is regularly employed. If a person named in a subpoena fails to attend or refuses to answer, enforcement must be sought from the issuing district court; the Board has no jurisdiction to enforce subpoenas. See Kellogg Co. v. New Generation Foods Inc. and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign person (party) — general rule for depositions taken in foreign country
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery deposition of a natural person residing in a foreign country who is a party (or officer/director/managing agent or Rule 30(b)(6)/31(a)(4) designee) shall, if taken in a foreign country, be taken in the manner prescribed by § 2.124 (i.e., on written questions) unless the Board, on motion for good cause, orders or the parties stipulate that the deposition be taken by oral examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if taken by written questions, parties may move the Board to allow oral examination for good cause or stipulate to oral. See TBMP § 703.01(b) for testimony depositions. Consult local counsel/Dept. of State about foreign law and procedures before attempting foreign depositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign law considerations and sanctions analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When foreign laws conflict with a party's discovery obligations, factors considered in imposing sanctions for non-compliance include: (1) the good faith of the non-complying party; (2) whether the non-complying party would incur foreign criminal liability; and (3) whether alternative sources of information are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should investigate the law and policy of the foreign country and consult the Office of Citizens Consular Services, Dept. of State, before seeking foreign depositions. Cases cited include Societe Internationale v. Rogers and Cochran Consulting Inc. v. Uwatec USA Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign willing nonparty depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery deposition of a natural person who resides in a foreign country and is not a party but is willing to appear voluntarily may be taken in the same manner as a foreign-party deposition (i.e., as described in TBMP § 404.03(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, some countries prohibit taking testimony within their boundaries for use in another country, or permit it only under certain procedures. Consult local counsel or Dept. of State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign unwilling nonparty — letter rogatory procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: An unwilling nonparty witness in a foreign country sometimes may be compelled to respond through the letter rogatory procedure: a written request routed through diplomatic channels to an appropriate foreign judicial authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure before the Board: file written request with Board, submit original and two copies of proposed letter rogatory and questions (and translations if required), serve copies on adverse parties. Adverse parties may submit cross-questions and propounding party may submit redirect questions. The Board issues the letter if approved as to form; the Board transmits to Dept. of State for diplomatic channels. The requesting party must pay fees (authentication, consular, foreign government) and make a deposit to cover consular/foreign fees. The process is uncertain, time-consuming (months to years), may suspend Board proceedings, and compliance is discretionary with foreign authorities. Even if honored, probative value may be limited because foreign authorities follow their own procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague Convention as alternative to letter rogatory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague Convention on the Taking of Evidence Abroad provides procedures (letter of request) under which a judicial authority in one member country may request evidence in another member country; it is another method to seek deposition of an unwilling nonparty if the foreign country is a Convention member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board has been advised foreign countries are more likely to assist under a formal letter rogatory; before filing under the Hague Convention consult Dept. of State about likelihood of compliance, especially when the Board (an administrative tribunal) would be the initiating authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign person present within the United States — depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a foreign party (or officer/director/managing agent or other person who consents to testify on its behalf) is or will be present in the U.S. during discovery, such person may be deposed by oral examination upon notice by the party seeking discovery (37 CFR § 2.120(c)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deposition must be taken in the federal judicial district where the witness resides or is regularly employed, or where the witness is at the time of the deposition. This option does not preclude other procedures described for foreign depositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons before whom depositions may be taken
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the United States, a deposition must be taken before: (A) an officer authorized to administer oaths either by federal law or by the law in the place of examination; or (B) a person appointed by the court where the action is pending to administer oaths and take testimony. In a foreign country a deposition may be taken under treaty or convention, under a letter of request, on notice before a person authorized to administer oaths by federal law or by the law of the place, or before a person commissioned by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fed. R. Civ. P. 28 controls; depositions must not be taken before a person who is any party's relative, employee, or attorney; who is related to or employed by any party's attorney, or who is financially interested in the action. In practice U.S. depositions for Board proceedings are usually before a court reporter authorized to administer oaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of deposition — content and special rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice must be reasonable written notice stating the time and place of the deposition and, if known, the deponent’s name and address; if the name is unknown, provide a general description sufficient to identify the person or class. A notice to a party deponent may be accompanied by a Rule 34 request to produce documents and tangible things at the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In its notice or subpoena a party may name an organization and must describe with reasonable particularity the matters for examination (Rule 30(b)(6)); the organization must designate one or more persons to testify on its behalf and may specify matters for each designated person. The persons designated must testify about information known or reasonably available to the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions upon written questions — 37 CFR § 2.124 filing and service rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A party desiring to take a discovery deposition upon written questions shall serve notice thereof upon each adverse party and shall file a copy of the notice, but not copies of the questions, with the Board. The notice shall state the name and address, if known, of the person to be deposed; if unknown, a general description sufficient to identify the person or class shall be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every notice under § 2.124(b) must be accompanied by the name or descriptive title of the officer before whom the deposition is to be taken (37 CFR § 2.124(c)). For procedure see TBMP § 404.07.
